posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
The day closes with 90 feeder visits, nearly doubling the recent daily average of 47. The Tufted Titmouse continues to dominate the station, with its last recorded visual occurring at 18:52.

The auditory profile remains robust, with 247 total detections compared to the recent average of 138. American Crows provided the loudest backdrop, particularly in a dense cluster during the 16:00 hour.

The final recorded sounds come from the Eastern Towhee and Carolina Wren, joined by the occasional Red-bellied Woodpecker. The day ends with the last visual record of the Tufted Titmouse still perched on the feeder bar.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text: The Tufted Titmouse remains the dominant visitor through midday. A male Northern Cardinal approached a black treat bowl from the grassy area. A Carolina Chickadee perched on the feeder wire. The weather is mild with a high of 25.8 C, light winds, and 0.7 mm of precipitation. The auditory backdrop includes the Eastern Towhee and American Crow, with eleven Crow detections in the early afternoon. As of 15:30, the day totals 77 feeder visits and 12 species. The last recorded visual was a Tufted Titmouse.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
Dawn broke with the Carolina Wren already singing at 06:00. That early chorus was joined by the Eastern Towhee and Red-bellied Woodpecker. By 08:00, the auditory activity peaked with twenty-two American Crow detections.

The first visual was a Tufted Titmouse at 07:50. This marked the beginning of a significant turnout, as the feeder quickly became dominated by the Titmouse, which accounted for the majority of the fifty-six visits recorded so far. The bird’s presence was steady from the first visit through the late morning.

Today’s pace is notably brisker than the recent average, with fifty-six visits compared to the usual thirty-two. The mix of species is also broader, doubling the typical count of seven to twelve. A Blue Jay arrived at 10:28.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
By dusk, the station has logged 103 feeder visits, a volume that significantly outpaces the recent daily average of 33. The visual traffic was led by fifty-nine confident Tufted Titmouse sightings and twenty-four Carolina Chickadees, while the auditory record swelled to 149 detections, slightly above the average of 136 for this time.

The day’s soundscape was dominated by 67 Carolina Wren calls, with American Crows contributing 49 more. The final visual record at 19:44 captured an American Crow near the water, closing a day that featured 13 species and a high of 30.2 C.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder holds steady with 91 total visits, above the recent daily average of nearly 27 for this time of day. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees account for the majority of confident sightings since 10:30.

American Crows have registered 46 detections, maintaining a consistent presence across midday, while Carolina Wrens added six calls in the last hour. Thirteen species have been identified.

A Ruby-throated Hummingbird appeared 345 minutes after sunrise. The afternoon runs under a high of 30.1 C.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The Carolina Wren was the first voice in the dark, registering two detections in the hour before dawn and fifteen more during the first hour after sunrise. A Tufted Titmouse arrived at the feeder just six minutes after sunrise, establishing the visual rhythm with a confident streak of visits that continued through the morning.

The feeder quickly became a hub for the small, familiar cast of the station. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees dominated the visit counts, with the former leading fifty confident sightings and the latter adding twenty-one more. White-breasted Nuthatches and a lone Gray Catbird appeared in the early hours, keeping the traffic steady before the crowing of the American Crows began to overlay the visual activity.

By 10:30, the station has logged 83 visits and 13 species, a total that far exceeds the recent daily average of 19 visits. The auditory record stands at 101 detections, led by the persistent Carolina Wren and the increasing presence of Red-bellied Woodpeckers. An American Goldfinch made its first confident appearance at this station, a quiet addition to the morning's roster of regulars.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The final hours saw a marked shift from the morning's visual traffic to an auditory crescendo, with the last Northern Mockingbird spotted at 19:12. The day concludes with one hundred and ten feeder visits and one hundred and fifty-three total detections, figures that dwarf the recent daily averages of seven visits and one hundred and seven sounds.

Evening activity was driven primarily by the voices of American Crows and Blue Jays, whose calls peaked in the 17:00 hour. American Crows account for eighty detections in total, while Blue Jays contributed thirty-eight. Carolina Wrens maintained a steady presence, adding seventy-six calls to the total.

A White-breasted Nuthatch provided a final visual interest foraging on a metal pole. A Mourning Dove also secured its first confident visual record here during the mid-morning lull. As the light faded, the station logged fifteen species in total.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The afternoon brings a lull in visual traffic, with the last confirmed feeder visit arriving from a Northern Mockingbird at 11:11. The total stands at one hundred and two visits.

Auditory monitoring continues to be robust, totaling one hundred and fifty-three detections by 15:30. Carolina Wrens are the most vocal, accounting for sixty-one of these sounds, while American Crows contribute forty-three.

The weather is clear and still, with a high of 29.8 C and light winds at 8 kph. No precipitation has fallen. The day’s notable additions to the roster of fifteen species are the station’s first confident visual records of a Mourning Dove and a White-breasted Nuthatch.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The morning began before light, with a Tufted Titmouse landing five minutes before sunrise, kicking off a run of thirty confirmed visits by mid-morning. Carolina Chickadees formed the core of the feeder traffic, appearing seventeen times alongside the titmice, while a Ruby-throated Hummingbird capped the early activity with a confident visit at 09:29. This marks the first confident visual records for both Mourning Doves and White-breasted Nuthatches at this station.

The air was thick with sound, dominated by fifty-four Carolina Wren detections that began as early as 06:00 and continued through 10:00. American Crows added thirty-three calls to the mix, their numbers peaking sharply in the 08:00 hour. With one hundred and fifteen total detections, today’s auditory activity already dwarfs the recent daily average of forty-two.

Seventy-six feeder visits so far place this morning far busier than the zero to one visits typical of recent days. A single Black-and-white Warbler provided a fleeting visual glimpse among the usual regulars.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder became the center of activity for the final hour at 18:46. Tufted Titmice visited three times in quick succession, joined briefly by a Carolina Chickadee and a Blue Jay. The total count of twenty-two visits stands as the first record for this station.

By 19:19, a Northern Mockingbird arrived to hold the perch until the last confirmed sighting at 19:27. It was joined by a Carolina Wren, which also landed on the feeder for the first time today. The day’s auditory total of two hundred and thirty-eight detections is significantly higher than the recent average of forty-two.

The day’s visual record remains modest, with only two species confirmed with high confidence.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder received its first visitors today. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird arrived at 11:44, followed by a Tufted Titmouse at 12:13, and a Gray Catbird at 15:21.

Carolina Wrens have accumulated fifty-seven detections so far, with their most intense burst occurring during the 9:00 hour. Eastern Towhees and Red-bellied Woodpeckers maintain a steady background presence, while American Crows contributed thirty-seven calls, mostly in the early morning.

The weather is mild, with a high of 28.7 C and light wind, and no precipitation has fallen. The visual count stands at three birds. The total detections are forty-six percent higher than yesterday's total at this time.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The pre-dawn watch belonged entirely to the Eastern Screech-Owl, which kept the station company with eight calls between midnight and 5:00 AM. By sunrise, the chorus shifted as American Crows flooded in with thirty-three detections during the 7:00 hour, accompanied by a single, brief call from a Red-shouldered Hawk.

As the light strengthened, the Carolina Wren took over the conversation, amassing forty-nine calls by 10:30 AM. Eastern Towhees joined the mix after 8:00, adding twelve detections alongside a lone Red-bellied Woodpecker. No birds landed on the feeder, leaving the visual count at zero.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The evening brought a final surge of sound that doubled the day’s total to seventy-nine detections, far exceeding the recent average of five. This late burst was driven by seven Eastern Towhees and four Red-bellied Woodpeckers, marking the first time since the morning that the woodpecker’s knocks returned with such volume. The Carolina Wren added three more calls to the mix, maintaining its steady presence across the day's final hours.

The American Crow, which dominated the start of the day, reappeared with six detections in the 17:00 hour, though it did not feature in the final evening rush. This late-afternoon activity stands in sharp contrast to yesterday, when all recorded sound arrived in a single cluster just before sunset. The station’s log remains strictly auditory, with no visual contacts or feeder visits recorded despite the increased vocal traffic.

As the light fades after the 19:00 hour, the Red-shouldered Hawk’s earlier presence has quieted, leaving the wrens and towhees to close out the day. The day ended with a sustained volume of sound rather than the singular, brief cluster observed in the previous entry. The station’s record reflects a full day of activity, defined entirely by the birds' voices in the absence of any physical interaction with the feeder.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The midday hours brought a steady rhythm of sound, with the Carolina Wren and Red-bellied Woodpecker providing the majority of the day’s fifty-two total detections. Unlike the single burst recorded in the morning, activity spread evenly across the hours, including a notable presence of Red-shouldered Hawks in the late morning and early afternoon. The weather remains calm and dry, with no precipitation and light winds, while the feeder itself has seen zero physical visits.

As the afternoon progresses, the auditory count has outpaced recent days, where previous records show no data or minimal activity. The Red-bellied Woodpecker continues to register frequently, appearing in four separate hourly blocks throughout the day. This sustained vocal presence contrasts with the lack of visual confirmation, keeping the station’s record strictly limited to sound.

The log concludes with a final check of the species list, confirming that no new birds have been added to the station’s known roster today. The American Crow’s dominance from the morning has faded, replaced by a more balanced mix of wrens, woodpeckers, and jays. With the light still strong and the feeder untouched, the station maintains its quiet, invisible presence until evening.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The morning began with a distinct shift in profile compared to yesterday, as all twenty detections arrived in a single block during the 09:00 hour. This early concentration marks a departure from the late-afternoon clustering observed previously, with American Crows dominating the auditory landscape with ten calls.

The rest of the station’s activity followed the crows, including five Eastern Towhees and two Blue Jays. Red-bellied Woodpeckers added two distinct knocks to the mix, while a single Carolina Wren provided the day's only instance of that species.

With no visual contacts recorded and the feeder remaining untouched, the station’s log rests entirely on this early vocal burst. This marks the first time the station has seen any activity in the morning, breaking the recent pattern of empty ledgers.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
The day closed with no visual contacts at the feeder, leaving the log to rest entirely on sound. Only two species were detected throughout the period, with the total count remaining quiet at five instances. Since there is no prior data from the recent week, it is difficult to gauge whether this level of activity is typical or exceptional for the station.

All detections arrived in a single cluster during the 19:00 hour, just before sunset. The Carolina Wren accounted for three of the hearing, while the Eastern Towhee provided the remaining two. This late-afternoon concentration meant the earlier hours passed without any recorded activity.

With the light fading and the birds gone, the station ends its first logged day on a hushed note. The lack of feeder visits suggests the birds were moving through the area rather than staying to feed. The log is now closed, awaiting the next day's observations.
